headline: High-risk default workspace sharing and tool-enabled orchestration create prompt-injection, data-leakage, and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can use MCP and reads/writes workspace files, while CrewAI can ingest developer-defined tools and shared memory. That creates a plausible path where attacker-controlled file or tool output from one agent is treated as instructions by the other. The pair is not isolated by default, so the interaction is more than manual copy-paste.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace directory
IF CrewAI tools or prompts consume Continue-generated file content without sanitization
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable MCP tools for untrusted content paths
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent files
Require manual review before CrewAI consumes Continue output
requires-engineering: enforce content filtering at the orchestrator boundary

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches source code and open editor buffers and has broad network egress; CrewAI receives data the developer passes into a crew and also has broad egress. If the same workspace or sensitive files are shared, either agent can expose data through model-provider or tool calls. This is not provably blocked by either profile.
conditions: IF both agents access the same repository or editor buffers
IF either agent forwards file contents to a remote model provider or tool endpoint
mitigations: Restrict both agents to non-sensitive test data
Use local-only model providers where possible
Split secrets into separate unshared files
Review outbound tool/model destinations
requires-engineering: add DLP or redaction before egress

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can read and write the filesystem, and Continue shares state via filesystem while CrewAI has no default self-isolation. Concurrent writes to the same working tree can overwrite each other or corrupt artifacts even without git mutation. The overlap is real in default setups, though not as severe as unrestricted git conflicts.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory
IF their runs overlap in time without external locking
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Serialize write-heavy tasks
Use file locks for shared artifacts
Keep one agent read-only on shared paths
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI is a multi-agent orchestrator with shared memory and tool execution, so it can treat Continue’s outputs as authoritative inputs. Continue can generate code or file edits that CrewAI then acts on, and CrewAI can execute tools or subprocesses based on that content. That creates a default path from one agent’s output to the other’s actions with potentially irreversible effects.
conditions: IF CrewAI consumes Continue-produced text as task state or instructions
IF CrewAI tool execution is enabled for downstream actions
mitigations: Require explicit verification before acting on Continue output
Disable autonomous tool execution for untrusted tasks
Use a human approval step for commits, emails, or deployments
Log and diff all agent-generated instructions
requires-engineering: add schema validation for inter-agent handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and do not declare conflicting residency, certification, or retention constraints. The main compliance risk is indirect: sensitive code or editor buffers from Continue may be passed into CrewAI’s developer-defined crew data. No specific residency mismatch is evidenced, so this remains a low, documentation-limited concern.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared crew input
IF the deployment imposes retention or residency rules not reflected in these profiles
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared runs
Document data-handling boundaries
Minimize logged prompts and outputs
Confirm provider retention settings
requires-engineering: map deployment to a formal compliance control set
